The following is hypothetical, since we do not have a proper safety report yet.

It sounds like the issue happened, because there was an error in the line-based train control system (LZB), which led to falling back to the point-based train control system (ASFA). However since there are more virtual blocks in LZB, than physical blocks in ASFA, this means that suddenly more than one train is in one block, which violates the most basic assumption of train control. That requires the trains to not rely on the train control at all, even if it says that the block is clear, but instead are operated manually.

I do not know what the proper procedures for that are in Spain, but in e.g. Germany that seems to require driving by sight. However that is also only after a number of accidents due this situation. So the following seem to be similar accidents from Germany:

- https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eisenbahnunfall_von_Meerbusch-...

- On April 9, 2002, a near-collision occurred near Fallersleben. After a computer at the LZB control center in Fallersleben crashed, two trains on each of the two main tracks came to a stop. When the computer was restarted, the rear train in each pair was signaled a speed of 160 km/h, while the front train in each pair was signaled 0 km/h. One of the two train operators following saw the train stopped in front of him; the other, as a precaution, contacted the operations center, which warned him not to proceed.

The level of human negligence here is astounding. The system did exactly what it was supposed to (lock the train down if the track can't be confirmed clear), and then a human controller ordered the crew to override the system, and ordered them to proceed at an unsafe speed towards a similarly disabled train?

It should not be possible for one person to make a mistake of this magnitude.
In case of a disconnected/off main safety system, the train should be limited on a hardware level to not be able to go over 40km/h.

Reading the text it seems to me this is due to a very widespread issue in Spain and other southern European countries: people don’t care about the warnings because there are too many false positives.

That’s why people here, when they hear the fire alarm they just wait for it to go off: the probability that it is actually a fire is minuscule… but the alarm triggers a lot.

Not sure how to actually solve this… but I’m also not making excuses for what happened. High speed trains is not the same as a fire alarm in some office building, the people in charge should be held responsible somehow.

I think aircraft are so safe in this regard because, essentially, they are required to use a single international collision avoidance system that is well defined. And modern cars have AEB systems built by vendors aiming for commonality to meet worldwide rules.

But train traffic systems seem to be a hodgepodge of different systems, perhaps locally grown and driven by the local vagaries of politics and rulemaking.

What a surprising inversion of expectations regarding safety.

I can't imagine what every passenger who survived and the families of those who passed are going through. Such a catastrophic incident with multiple human failures is so tragic and so needless. From the controller to the driver, every single one of them should have said hey we shouldn't just ignore a signal and should investigate why it's on first. For this to be such a quick decision suggests it's not a one off. I would be extremely interested to see how many near misses or ignored signals there has been across Spain. The crash earlier this year was due to inexperienced workers and it seems as if significant training improvements and protocols are needed.

I still don't know why the train drivers don't have a simple data: 
  The distance to the train that is next in in that railway in its direction.
With this information, that accident will have never happened.

This accident seems to have been caused by human error. Moreover, (from the news) the working arrangements and procedures seem to be such that in the event of a controller (or driver) making a mistake there was no automatic failsafe protection in place to stop the Renfe train.

An automatic failsafe mechanism should be installed to stop/cut the power to the moving train in situations like this, it should work irrespective of any instructions or actions by the controller or the driver.

When safety parameters deemed the Renefe train to be travelling too fast and too close to the Iryo one it should have stopped automatically. Such safety measures aren't rocket science but straightforward engineering, (interlocks, etc.). Over the years there have been too many accidents in situations such as this for such equipment not to be installed.

For a moment I visualized myself in that busy control room and easily making that mistake even though I'd made the correct decision hundreds of times previously. Not only are 69 lost lives a terrible tragedy but the life of the person who made this momentary slip has been ruined forever.

It should not have been allowed to happen. It's worth remembering that Westinghouse brake systems (which are well over a century old) automatically default to on (stop) when there's a fault, and the high speed (now decades old) Shinkansen has very sophisticated stopping mechanisms and has never had a major crash. The question is why such safety measures weren't installed here.
At least California's high-speed rail will never kill anyone.

Obviously train safety systems should be formally verified and eliminate human error (only permit safe leeway to humans).

But apart from the safety mechanisms, there is also the concept of securing passengers.

What we know so far is that originally, cars weren't equipped with safety belts, until they were.

Imagine a thought experiment: the trains are equipped with safety belts, on a voluntary basis. Initially everyone scoffs at them, except for a minority. Time passes until an accident happens. Then everybody learns that the forward facing passengers that were facing forward had the lowest casualty reports, next are the people facing backwards, since a decelerating train mostly just pushes them harder into their own seats, and their safety depends on the discipline of any occupant who happens to sit on the forward facing seat. People start preferring the safest seats forward facing with belts (you only depend on your own discipline). People sitting in a forwards facing seat who refuse to put on the belt will be asked to find a different seat or put on the belt. In many places it will turn out a lot of passengers are standing upright "by necessity" even though no law of nature or authority mandates or permits railroad operators to sell more tickets than they have safe seats. But first that would require figuring out what new lucrative job prospects can be opened for insurance companies, and any population around the world may think out loud why insurance on offenses appear to be legal and often even encouraged by court systems!

It turns out its never really possible to draw an objective line between accidental and intentional offenses, so at a fundamental level we should either permit insurance that covers you when caught committing murder, grand larceny or what have you (done); OR we should ban all insurance from covering offenses (accidental and intentional). Insurance "allows the system to stably continue without shocks reverberating through the economy in the face of adverse events" is a poor justification for permitting the insurance of offenses, especially since it typically results in the wrong questions being asked, and instead of figuring out who paid the least to insurance scams, perhaps some real questions could delve up real solutions that save lives instead of defend the income streams of lawyers profiting on the misery of civilians.

This event was pretty chilling for me because I just took the Renfe line from Seville to Madrid a couple of weeks ago while visiting Spain. I generally like to think that I have a pretty good instinct on relative risks and make reasonable decisions based on that. This time around, between the incident earlier this year and this most recent incident, depending on how you interpret and apply the statistics (of course that's always up for healthy debate), it looks like it would have actually been safer driving between Seville and Madrid. That's a pretty low bar in terms of safety!

I set my favorite agent on the task (Opus 5.5 in the Kagi Assistant), and given the two rail crashes in Spain this year, these are the stats it came up with for "chances of dying" via various modes of transportation between Seville and Madrid:

* EU high-speed rail, long-run average: ~1 in 36 million

* This rail line, counting both 2026 crashes: ~1 in 400,000 to 1.2 million (prior to the most recent crash it was 1–3 million; now ~2.5× higher)

* Flying with a European airline: ~1 in 80 million

* Driving: ~1 in 1 million or worse

Of course this is hindsight. Heightened awareness of risks, higher propensity to overreact to anomalies or alarms, procedural changes, and so forth in the wake of this second crash might push high-speed rail in Spain to be higher than the European average in the future.
